name: Cica / Centella asiatica
lead: Cica is the skincare shorthand for Centella asiatica, a perennial herb also called gotu kola or Asiatic pennywort. Its extracts and isolated triterpenoids (asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid and madecassic acid) are put into soothing creams, serums and masks that people use to calm irritated skin and to help skin recover after blemishes, wounds and scarring, leaving a smoother, calmer-looking complexion.[1][2]

Reviews describe laboratory and clinical work in which the plant's triterpenes promote fibroblast proliferation and collagen synthesis and improve the strength of newly formed skin, and they discuss its use in small wounds, hypertrophic scars, burns, photoaging and stretch marks.[2][3] Wikipedia reports that the plant has traditional use for skin conditions and minor wounds, while noting that clinical efficacy and safety have not been established in clinical research.[1]
Cica is often printed on packaging as 'cica' or paired with madecassoside. No clinical study of cica specifically for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation was located.

paras: Cica products are used topically to soothe sensitive or irritated skin and to support recovery after blemishes, scrapes and scarring.[1][2] A review of Centella asiatica in cosmetology says the extract has been examined for photoaging skin, cellulite and stretch marks, with a mechanism that involves increased collagen synthesis and fibronectin content.[3]

The plant has been used for centuries in folk medicine, described in one review as a 'panacea' 3000 years ago, and is eaten as a leafy green in several Asian cuisines.[1][2] Reviews also report ethnomedicinal use in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine, including for memory and brain function.[4]

The plant is native to tropical regions of Africa, Asia, Australia and western Pacific islands and grows in swampy areas. About 124 compounds have been identified, chiefly triterpenoids and their glycosides.[1] Asiaticoside and madecassoside are the marker compounds named in the Chinese Pharmacopoeia.[4]

Laboratory and animal work reported in reviews describes promotion of fibroblast proliferation, increased collagen and fibronectin synthesis, better tensile strength of newly formed skin, and dampening of the inflammatory phase in hypertrophic scars and keloids.[2][3] Reviews of asiaticoside and madecassoside list anti-inflammatory, antioxidant and wound-healing activities among their reported properties.[4]

Reviews of the topical literature summarise experimental and clinical work on wound healing, hypertrophic scars and burns,[2][5][6] and a 2024 systematic review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included Centella asiatica among the botanicals it compared.[7] No studies found of Centella asiatica specifically for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Wikipedia states that clinical efficacy and safety of the plant have not been proven in clinical research.[1]

Topical use can cause contact dermatitis and irritation, and eating it may cause drowsiness. Reviews published in 2024 linked foods and supplements containing the plant to jaundice and liver disease, with case reports of liver disease after several weeks of use.[1]

card.summary: The gotu kola plant behind 'cica' skincare, a traditional soothing herb with no located trials for pigment recovery.
card.aka: Gotu kola, Asiatic pennywort, madecassoside, asiaticoside
card.note: Topical contact dermatitis reported; oral products linked to liver injury case reports.

quick.overview:
Cica is skincare shorthand for Centella asiatica, or gotu kola, a herb used traditionally for skin conditions and minor wounds. Its extracts appear in soothing creams and serums.

Wikipedia notes that clinical efficacy and safety have not been proven in clinical research, and no study on pigment recovery was found.
quick.mechanism: Its main active compounds are triterpenoids such as asiaticoside and madecassoside; the sources reviewed do not describe a pigment mechanism.
quick.risks: Topical use can cause contact dermatitis or irritation. Oral products have been linked in case reports to liver disease and may cause drowsiness.

chain: Triterpenes soothe irritation and support wound repair
Calmer skin and tidier healing of blemishes and small wounds
Less visible redness and marking, smoother-looking skin
angle.text: People apply cica products to calm redness and support skin as it heals after breakouts or minor injuries, aiming for a more even, less irritated complexion. It is used as a soothing layer in routines alongside moisturisers and sunscreen.
